46_marg3136: The Lord is a jealous God. Here begins the prophecy, which has two parts. In the first chapter he treats of the destruction of Sennacherib and his people; in the two following, of the laying waste of Ninive and the passing of the kingdom of the Assyrians to the Chaldeans. In this first chapter, then, he describes, first, the anger of the Lord and the power he will use against the Assyrians; and from this, second, he comforts the Jews, that that wrath is not coming upon them: The Lord is good. Third, he shows why and how Sennacherib is to be driven out and destroyed: What do ye devise. Fourth, he comforts the Jews by delivering them from so great an army: I have afflicted thee. Fifth, he foretells the flight and death of Sennacherib and the manner of his death: And the Lord will give a commandment. Sixth, he fully comforts the Jews, wholly delivered: Behold upon the mountains. He says, then: the Lord is jealous, that is, a vehement lover of his own, namely the Jews.

46_marg3190: Allegorically. The world, which “is seated in wickedness” and kills men with its tongues, is called the city of blood; it is lying in the perversity of the teachings by which it tears and carries off many. In the world too is the noise of the whip, that is, of the tribulations under which the just cry out when they are afflicted: when one is tormented by anger, another by lust, another by hatred or envy, the whip of the Assyrian king sounds in them. Sometimes the devil's whip is felt in bodily diseases; for sometimes, not from the nature of the elements but from the devil striking, jaundice is sent, or dropsy, or the pain of the stone, and the like. In the world there is also the rattling of the wheel, when men, not knowing where safety is and where danger, run to and fro. There is also the neighing horse, that is, the devil, who fiercely pursues those who flee, tramples them and mocks them. There is also the running chariot, which is drowned with Pharao; it is drawn by four horses, that is, by the four passions of the mind. Hence: “Hence they desire and fear, grieve and rejoice.” In Ninive there sounds also the horseman coming up, that is, the devil, whose sword shines with the art of dialectic and rhetoric, and his spear glitters while he “transformeth himself into an angel of light”; and by these arms many are killed; and unless they are at once healed by grace, there is a grievous destruction, in which there is no end, because malice has no end. These evils fall, that is, they befall, on the bodies of the dead, which are laid low by the multiplying of fornication. And in Ninive there is a harlot, beautiful and agreeable, who draws almost everyone to love of her by various witchcrafts. She sells the nations in fornications, namely when, through love of temporal things and weariness of good things, those who had been members of Christ become “the members of an harlot,” and draw others with them.

How much more, then, will you unbelievers, who cling to the world, feel punishments and be despised? And you will seek help from the enemy, that the vices and demons may cease to pursue you; but all your strong holds, worldly sweetness, power, teachings, will be devoured by the devil, the eater, at the first shaking of the tree.

46_marg3202: Morally. Ninive, which is called beautiful, signifies the soul, by nature fair, which, clinging to pleasures, is unmanned, and opens the gates of the senses to vices and demons. For if anyone is a lover of pleasures more than of God, he has opened the gates of his land to the enemy; and the bars of this Babylon will be consumed by fire, that is, the natural good of the soul, by which it could shut against the enemy the road of the bodily senses. To her it is said that she should draw to herself the water of the divine word as a wall, and hold fast the natural good of the soul as it were, so that the enemy may not break through to the inner parts. There follows: Go into the clay: that is, you who have entangled yourself in various evils, bear patiently the wrongs of temptation; otherwise you will perish and lose all your natural good. Against these things, multiply yourself in as great a number of virtues as is the number of the bruchus.
46_marg3203: Allegorically. O Ninive, your people, that is, all worldly men, are so enervated by vices that they have nothing manly. Hence the enemies, namely the demons, or the vices, have entered through the open bodily senses; and they also, like fire, devour the natural power of knowing God, which ought to have barred the gates of the senses. Against these evils draw water for yourself: sprinkle yourself with the word and with reason; exercise yourself in the knowledge of God through the virtues planted in you; and do penance for having fallen. This is what he says: Go into the clay: bear the wrong patiently, and the necessity of the body in which you are wrapped; and, working it, that is, bringing into servitude the brick, that is, the body, tread it and hold it, so that it does not rule over you; because, if you remain there, that is, in the body, the living flame either of the vices here, or of hell hereafter, will consume you; and you will perish by the sword, that is, by the violent assault of the devil. And, after the likeness of locusts, whatever seemed green in you, and the good of nature springing up of itself, is consumed by the bruchus eating it. But so that this may not happen, multiply yourself in virtues as innumerable as the bruchus. All these punishments you have suffered because you have multiplied your merchandises above the stars of heaven: because you gathered for yourself perishing riches by right and wrong; or you thought various teachings brighter than the stars; and, walking by the broad way, running to and fro in the softness of your opinion, you raised yourself to the heights; and your guards, that is, those set over you, were like locusts, raising themselves to the flight of heresy, but quickly falling down; and your little ones, that is, those born of the locusts, were like the attelebus, lifting themselves a little from the ground, so that at last they may grow into a locust. These, lacking the warmth of the true sun, sit on thorny seats, that is, the rough opinions of the philosophers. But when the sunrise comes, that is, the judgement of true knowledge, they leave their thorns and pass into pure and free flight.

46_marg3208: Since up to here the ruin of the world has been spoken of, at the end the wound of the devil himself is spoken of, who was the prince of the world and boasted that he ruled in it; to whom this apostrophe is made: O Lucifer, you are crushed; destroyed is Ninive, your beautiful and powerful city, in which you set yourself even against the Son of God. The shepherds who fed the people, not for salvation but so that you might devour them, have failed. The crowd of the people that worshipped you, leaving you and your city, has fled to the hiding places of the mountains, that is, of the apostles, and there is none of your leaders to call back to himself the crowd that was once yours. Your wound has resounded through the whole world. All insult you who before were deceived by your tripping. For there is no one, or scarcely anyone, whom you have not at some time deceived. He in whom the malice of the devil does not stay, but passes, can insult him, and clap over him with good works as with outstretched hands.
